Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 59
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Professor
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 54

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Visual (Water/Flooding): Water, flooding, or large bodies of water, Olfactory (Smell): Related smells, Stress: Stress
  Threat: Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Vignette:
Kwame Asante is a 59-year-old Ghanaian-born professor of African studies at a mid-sized university in the American Midwest, single, and widely regarded by colleagues as a composed and intellectually formidable presence in the department. He presented for psychological assessment approximately fourteen months after the event that fractured that composure — the near-drowning of his younger brother, Kofi, during catastrophic flash flooding that struck their family's home region in Ghana while Kwame was visiting during the summer academic break.

The flooding came without adequate warning in the early morning hours. Kwame had been asleep in the family compound when the water rose with terrifying speed, surging through doorways and filling the lower rooms within minutes. He found Kofi — twelve years his junior and the person he described as his closest living relative — face-down and unresponsive in chest-deep, debris-filled water in what had been the kitchen. Kwame pulled him free and performed resuscitation on a raised concrete platform while the water continued to climb around them, the smell of the flood — a dense, organic rot of soil, sewage, and river silt — filling everything. Kofi survived, but spent three weeks in a Ghanaian hospital with pulmonary complications, and Kwame returned to the United States before his brother was fully discharged, a fact that had settled into him like a stone.

In the months that followed, the symptoms arrived in layers. Back in the Midwest, Kwame discovered that the retention pond visible from the window of his faculty office — a feature he had never previously noticed — had become unbearable to look at. On mornings when rain was heavy and the pond swelled toward its banks, he found himself unable to sit at his desk. The physical reaction came before any conscious thought: his heart was already hammering, his hands already damp, before his mind had registered what his eyes had seen. He described this as deeply disorienting for a man who had built his professional identity around careful, deliberate reasoning — his body, he said, had stopped waiting for him.

The smell was perhaps the most invasive trigger. A particular combination of standing water and mud — encountered near campus drainage ditches after heavy rain, or even in the damp corner of a university basement — could return him instantly to that kitchen, to Kofi's weight in his arms, to the certainty in that moment that his brother was dead. He had begun taking longer routes across campus to avoid low-lying areas after rainfall, and had declined two departmental social events held near the university's lakeside conference centre. Colleagues had noticed the pattern without understanding it, and one had made a remark, half-joking, about Kwame becoming a recluse. The remark stung because it was not entirely wrong.

Stress itself had become a trigger of a different kind. During a particularly fraught faculty meeting involving a tenure dispute, Kwame felt the same flooding of fear and horror that he associated with the night in Ghana — a wave of emotion that seemed entirely disproportionate to the room he was sitting in. He had excused himself and stood in a corridor for several minutes, ashamed and bewildered. He had come to believe that something in him had been permanently altered, that the careful emotional regulation he had cultivated over decades was no longer reliably available to him. The guilt about leaving Ghana before Kofi was discharged had not diminished; if anything, it had grown more textured and insistent over time, accompanied by a shame he found difficult to articulate — a sense that he had not been, in the end, the man his brother needed him to be.

Even at home in the evenings, in what he knew to be a safe and familiar environment, Kwame could not fully settle. He remained in a state of low-level vigilance that exhausted him without ever resolving into rest.

What finally brought him to the clinic was a phone call from Kofi, who told him, gently, that Kwame sounded like a man waiting for something terrible to happen. Kwame had not been able to disagree. What he feared most, sitting in the intake room, was that this was simply who he was now. What he hoped for, more quietly, was to be proven wrong.
